lead: Easter is not a place to stop. Hebrews urges believers to move on from the first lessons of faith toward maturity, and warns of ground that drinks the rain and yields only thorns. Luke tells of a friend who knocks at midnight and will not go away, and promises that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Growth comes from asking and receiving. The key words are perfection, rain and ask.

r.h: Let us go on toward perfection
set: Just before this passage the writer has scolded his hearers: by now they ought to be teachers, yet they still need milk and not solid food (5:11–14). So he resolves to lead them on. The six items he lists in 6:1–2 are the basics that a new Christian learned before and around Baptism.

Then comes one of the hardest passages in the New Testament, on those who have fallen away. It must be read with the verse that follows it: “Even though we speak in this way, beloved, we are confident of better things in your case” (6:9). The warning is meant to wake people up, not to drive them to despair.
str: vv. 1–3: move beyond the foundation, which has six parts.
vv. 4–6: the danger of falling away after receiving so much.
vv. 7–8: a picture from farming: the same rain, two kinds of ground.
kw: The state of the grown-up believer, able to take solid food. It is the same family of words used of Christ “made perfect” (5:9).

Early Christians used “enlightenment” as a name for Baptism. St Justin Martyr says so in the second century, and the Catechism repeats it (CCC 1216). The list in vv. 4–5 describes the gifts of Christian initiation.
Not an ordinary sin of weakness, but a deliberate turning away from Christ after knowing him, as if crucifying the Son of God again (6:6).
vv: Therefore let us go on toward perfection,
The writer says “let us”: he includes himself. Growth in faith is a road all of us walk together.
instruction about baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment.
The “laying on of hands” was linked with the gift of the Spirit after Baptism (see Acts 8:17), the root of what our Church gives in Holy Mooron.
For it is impossible to restore again to repentance those who have once been enlightened,

Many Fathers, among them St John Chrysostom, read this as meaning that Baptism cannot be given a second time, not that repentance is closed (in substance). The person who refuses Christ cannot be brought back by human effort while he goes on refusing.
Ground that drinks up the rain falling on it repeatedly, and that produces a crop useful to those for whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God.
The rain is the same for both fields. What differs is the crop. Grace is given generously, and it asks for a harvest.
ch: The Church has always rejected the view that sins after Baptism cannot be forgiven. The Catechism says that there is no offence, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive, and that the door of forgiveness stays open to all who turn back (CCC 982). It also teaches that Baptism is given once and cannot be repeated, because it marks the soul with a seal (CCC 1272). The passage is therefore a call to perseverance, and the sacrament of Penance is the Lord's answer to those who fall.

set: Right after giving the Lord's Prayer, Jesus teaches how to pray it. In a village of his day, guests arrived at any hour, and hospitality was a duty for the whole community. A family's bread was baked for the day, and at night the house was shut, with the family sleeping together in one room. A friend who knocked would wake everyone.
Luke alone has the parable of the friend at midnight. The sayings that follow (vv. 9–13) are found also in Matthew 7:7–11.
str: vv. 11–13: from human fathers to the heavenly Father.
kw: Literally “shamelessness”. The man at the door does not stand on dignity. Jesus praises a prayer that is not too proud to keep knocking.
Three verbs in the present tense, which in Greek suggests going on doing them: keep asking, keep searching, keep knocking.
Where Matthew says the Father gives “good things” (Matthew 7:11), Luke says he gives the Holy Spirit. The best gift is God himself.
vv: Friend, lend me three loaves of bread;
He asks not for himself but for a guest. Prayer for others has a special place in this parable.
at least because of his persistence he will get up and give him whatever he needs.
The argument is from the lesser to the greater. If a sleepy neighbour gives in, how much more will God, who does not sleep and is not annoyed by our asking.
Ask, and it will be given you; search, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened for you.
The verbs are passive in the first and third lines: “it will be given”, “will be opened”. The giver is God.
how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!
This is the promise of Pentecost, already spoken on the road to Jerusalem. In Qyomtho we ask for the Spirit day by day.
ch: The Catechism groups three parables of Luke on prayer: the friend at midnight, the widow and the judge, and the Pharisee and the tax collector (CCC 2613). St Augustine, writing to the widow Proba, explains that God does not need to be told our wants; he wants our desire to grow through prayer, so that we may be able to receive what he is ready to give (Letter 130, in substance).

qa: Does Hebrews 6 mean that a Christian who falls into serious sin cannot be forgiven?

No. The Church teaches that every sin can be forgiven to one who repents (CCC 982), and the Lord gave the sacrament of Penance for those who fall after Baptism. Hebrews warns about a hardened turning away from Christ. As long as a person refuses him, no one can bring that person back; but God's door is never shut to the one who knocks.
rite: Today the Panchangam remembers Mar Shemun Bar Sabbae (Simeon bar Sabbae), bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, the capital of the Persian empire, who was put to death with many companions under King Shapur II in the fourth century. The ancient accounts tell that he refused to force his people to pay a crushing double tax laid on Christians, and that an aged court official who had denied the faith repented on seeing him and died a martyr too. He is honoured by the Syriac Churches of East and West, and he is a living picture of Hebrews 6: the one who had fallen came back.
study: Since Easter, have I grown, or have I settled down? What one step toward maturity can I take this week?
For whom am I knocking at God's door at midnight? Do I keep knocking?
